Athletics coach's note, district relay camp, Week 3.
When I paired Reena from the city convent school with Uday from the municipal school for baton practice, both rolled their eyes. Reena told her friends he “won't know the rules”. Uday's group called her “madam”.
On day two, they dropped the baton four times, blaming each other. On day four, Reena noticed Uday's handoff was faster than hers. She asked him to show her. He did, slowly.
Yesterday, their relay team beat the camp record. I saw Reena share her water bottle with Uday's whole group, laughing at a joke in Marathi she only half understood.
Next week I will mix all relay pairs across schools.

qa.a: Working toward a shared goal, the relay record, softened the bias between Reena and Uday, so mixing all pairs should do the same.

Thursday
Ms Kapoor paired me with Vaibhav for the science exhibition. Vaibhav. The back-bench gang, always laughing, never studying. I nearly cried.
Day one he came late. I said nothing and did the report. Day two our circuit wouldn't light up, and I was ready to give up. He looked at it for one minute, twisted two wires and it glowed. He said his father fixes fans and he's been doing it since he was small.
Today we worked through lunch. He explained current better than our textbook does. His friends kept calling him from the door, and he said, “Busy, yaar.”
I don't think I'll call them the back-bench gang any more. At least not him.
Ankita

For years the boys of Khedi and Pipariya had called each other names across the river. Khedi said Pipariya boys were thieves; Pipariya said Khedi boys were show-offs. Vijay had never spoken to one.
Then the block school merged the two kabaddi squads for the district tournament, and the coach put Vijay beside Manoj from Pipariya on the left flank. The first week they barely looked at each other. Manoj tackled late; Vijay muttered under his breath.
In the quarter-final at Sehore, Manoj held the raider's ankle just long enough for Vijay to lock him. They won by one point. On the tractor-trolley ride home, Manoj shared his roasted chana, and Vijay learned he wanted to be a vet, like Vijay's own cousin.
Back in Khedi, when his friend Raju started on "those Pipariya thieves", Vijay said, "Manoj isn't. Say something else."

qa.a: By one point.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel about Manoj in the first week?
qa.a: Vijay was wary and irritated, muttering at Manoj's late tackles, because Manoj was still just a boy from the other village.

qa.q: What changed Vijay's view, and what could others learn from it?
qa.a: Working toward the same win, then talking on the ride home; a shared goal turns a label into a person.

qa.q: How might Raju react to Vijay's reply?
qa.a: Raju may be surprised or a bit put out, since Vijay used to share the joke, but now the label has a real face.
